chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was MESSENGER launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s MESSENGER spacecraft orbited Mercury for more than four years. Among its accomplishments, the mission determined Mercury’s surface composition, revealed its geological history, discovered details about its internal magnetic field, and verified its polar deposits are dominantly water-ice.
MESSENGER launched in 2004 (Aug. 2, 2004), bound for Mercury.

chapters.caption: MESSENGER — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is MESSENGER?
paragraphs: MESSENGER (Mercury Surface, Space Environment, Geochemistry and Ranging) was the seventh Discovery-class mission, and the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury.
After that, its PAM-D solid motor fired to put the spacecraft on an escape trajectory into heliocentric orbit at 0.92 × 1.08 AU and 6.4 degrees inclination to the ecliptic.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did MESSENGER get to Mercury?
paragraphs: MESSENGER was launched at 06:15:57 UT Aug. 3, 2004, into an initial parking orbit around Earth.

The six-and-a-half-year road to Mercury was punctuated by several gravity-assist maneuvers through the inner solar system, including one flyby of Earth (Aug. 2, 2005), two flybys of Venus (Oct. 24, 2006, and June 5, 2007), and three flybys of Mercury (Jan. 14, 2008, Oct. 6, 2008, and Sept. 29, 2009).

chapters.caption: MESSENGER Encounters the Innermost Planet

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has MESSENGER taught us?
paragraphs: During the second Venusian flyby (at a range of only 210 miles or 338 kilometers), MESSENGER relayed back a vast amount of data, including visible and near-infrared imaging data on the upper atmosphere.
The three Mercury flybys further slowed the spacecraft, although, during the last encounter in September 2009, MESSENGER entered a safe mode and, as a result, collected no data on Mercury.

chapters.caption: Where is MESSENGER?

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is MESSENGER now?
paragraphs: The mission ended when MESSENGER slammed into Mercury’s surface.
MESSENGER finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Mariner 10 launched?
paragraphs: Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft sent to the planet Mercury; the first mission to explore two planets (Mercury and Venus) during a single mission; the first to return to its primary destination for another look; and the first to use a gravity assist to change its flight path.
Mariner 10 launched in 1973 (Nov. 3, 1973), bound for Mercury.

chapters.question: What is Mariner 10?
paragraphs: Soon after leaving Earth orbit, the spacecraft returned striking photos of both Earth and the Moon as it sped to its first destination, Venus.
Mariner 10 is a multiple flybys built by NASA to study Mercury.

chapters.question: Why was BepiColombo launched?
paragraphs: BepiColombo is an international mission comprised of two spacecraft riding together to Mercury to orbit and to study the planet from unique vantage points.

BepiColombo is an international mission comprised of two spacecraft riding together to Mercury to orbit and to study the planet from unique vantage points. The European Space Agency (ESA) provided one orbiter. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) supplied the second orbiter.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is BepiColombo?
paragraphs: The European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) each have an orbiter on the same spacecraft.
ESA built the main spacecraft, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and JAXA supplied the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO).

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did BepiColombo get to Mercury?
paragraphs: BepiColombo made its first flyby of Mercury on Oct. 1, 2021, and sent back several images.
Several more planetary flybys will be used to steer BepiColombo into orbit around Mercury in November 2026.

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is BepiColombo now?
paragraphs: A few months before going into orbit, BepiColombo will jettison the spacecraft’s transfer module leaving the two orbiters – still connected to each other – to be captured by Mercury’s gravity.
BepiColombo is still exploring Mercury today, 8 years after launch. Its data keeps arriving and the team keeps finding new uses for it.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Venus Express launched?
paragraphs: Venus Express was the first European spacecraft to orbit Venus. The original mission was expected to last no more than 500 Earth days, but the mission was extended five times.
Venus Express launched in 2005 (Nov. 9, 2005), bound for Venus.
chapters.imageAlt: Launch Vehicles (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Launch Vehicles

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Venus Express?
paragraphs: ESA’s Venus Express was designed to study the atmosphere of Venus, its plasma environment and surface characteristics from a 24-hour near-polar elliptical orbit.
The spacecraft was launched by a Soyuz-FG/Fregat combination owned by Starsem, a French company which markets a European version of the Russian Soyuz.
chapters.imageAlt: Venus Express from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Venus Express — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Venus Express get to Venus?
paragraphs: The Soyuz-FG delivered the payload into a low Earth orbit, with the Fregat firing a second time 96 minutes after launch to send the entire stack out of Earth orbit toward Venus.
The spacecraft arrived at Venus on April 11, 2006, after a five-month journey.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Venus - Multiple Views of High-level Clouds

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Venus Express taught us?
paragraphs: Other major findings included evidence for past oceans on the surface of Venus, a higher prevalence of lightning on Venus than Earth, and the discovery of a huge double atmospheric vortex at the south pole of the planet.
In 2011, scientists studying data from Venus Express reported the existence of a layer of ozone in the upper atmosphere.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Four Views of Venus High Pass Filter

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Venus Express now?
paragraphs: The original Venus Express mission was planned to last no more than 500 Earth days, but the mission was extended five times: to May 2009, to December 2009, to December 2012, to 2014 and finally to 2015.
Venus Express finished its mission in 2006. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Pioneer Venus 2 launched?
paragraphs: Pioneer Venus 2, the sistership to Pioneer Venus 1, consisted of the main spacecraft, a large probe, and three identical small probes—all designed to collect data as they descended toward the surface of Venus. Amazingly two probes survived the hard impact and one transmitted data from the surface for 67.5 minutes.
Pioneer Venus 2 launched in 1978 (Aug. 8, 1978), bound for Venus.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Launch Vehicles

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Pioneer Venus 2?
paragraphs: Pioneer Venus 2, the sistership to Pioneer Venus 1, consisted of the main spacecraft, a Large Probe (698 pounds or 316.5 kilograms), and three identical Small Probes, all of which were designed to collect data during entry into the atmosphere of Venus.
The probes were shaped like cones and were not expected to survive impact with the surface.

chapters.caption: Pioneer Venus 2 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Pioneer Venus 2 get to Venus?
paragraphs: It landed at 4.4 degrees north latitude and 304 degrees east longitude at a velocity of 20 miles per hour (32 kilometers per hour).
The three Small Probes (2.5 feet or 76 centimeters in diameter) arrived in the atmosphere within minutes of the bigger one and descended rapidly without the benefit of parachutes.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Venus - Multiple Views of High-level Clouds

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Pioneer Venus 2 taught us?
paragraphs: The so-called Day Probe transmitted data from the surface for 67 minutes, 37 seconds, before succumbing to the high temperatures, pressures and power depletion.
The main spacecraft, meanwhile, burned up in the atmosphere at an altitude of about 75 miles (120 kilometers)—about 1.5 hours after the probes—and provided key data on higher regions.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Four Views of Venus High Pass Filter

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Pioneer Venus 2 now?
paragraphs: Using a combination of air drag and a parachute, the Large Probe descended through the atmosphere, entering at a velocity of 7 miles per second (11.6 kilometers per second), slowing down until it impacted on the surface of Venus at 19:40 UT.
Pioneer Venus 2 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.question: Why was Pioneer Venus 1 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Pioneer Venus 1 was the first of a two-spacecraft orbiter-probe combination designed to study the atmosphere of Venus. It was the first American spacecraft to orbit Venus. The second spacecraft was launched a few months later.
Pioneer Venus 1 launched in 1978 (May 20, 1978), bound for Venus.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Pioneer Venus 1?
paragraphs: Formally approved by NASA in August 1974, the Pioneer Venus project comprised two spacecraft to explore the atmosphere and surface of Venus.
Both spacecraft used a basic cylindrical bus.

chapters.caption: Pioneer Venus 1 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Pioneer Venus 1 get to Venus?
paragraphs: Pioneer Venus 1, the orbiter, was designed to spend an extended period in orbit around Venus mapping the surface using a radar package.
After a six-and-a-half-month journey, the spacecraft entered an elliptical orbit around Venus at 15:58 UT Dec. 4, 1978.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Venus - Multiple Views of High-level Clouds

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Pioneer Venus 1 taught us?
paragraphs: Data from the radar mapper allowed scientists to produce a topographical map of most of the Venusian surface between 73 degrees north latitude and 63 degrees south latitude at a resolution of about 47 miles (75 kilometers).
The data indicated that Venus was much more smooth and spherical than Earth.

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Pioneer Venus 1 now?
paragraphs: In May 1992, Pioneer Venus 1 began the final phase of its mission, maintaining its periapsis between 93 and 155 miles (150 and 250 kilometers) until propellant depletion.
Pioneer Venus 1 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.question: Why was Mariner 5 launched?
paragraphs: Originally built as a backup to the successful Mariner 4 mission to Mars in 1965, Mariner 5 was modified to fly by Venus. The spacecraft’s flight path after its Venus encounter brought it closer to the Sun than any previous mission at the time.
Mariner 5 launched in 1967 (June 14, 1967), bound for Venus.

chapters.question: What is Mariner 5?

Unlike Mariner 4, however, Mariner 5 did not carry an imaging instrument.

paragraphs: NASA’s Mariner 2 was humanity’s first successful planetary science mission. The first close-up look at another planet was full of surprises: Mariner 2 found Venus to be inhospitable, and far hotter than expected.
Mariner 2 launched in 1962 (Aug. 27, 1962), bound for Venus.

Mariner 2 is a flyby built by NASA to study Venus.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Magellan launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Magellan mission to Venus was one of the most successful deep space missions. It was the first spacecraft to image the entire surface of Venus and made several discoveries about the planet. Magellan burned up about 10 hours after being commanded to plunge into the Venusian atmosphere.
Magellan launched in 1989 (May 4, 1989), bound for Venus.

chapters.caption: Magellan Orbit Artist Concept

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Magellan?
paragraphs: Magellan, named after the Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan (1480-1521), was the first deep space probe launched by the United States in almost 11 years, and also the first probe launched by a space shuttle.
Magellan was designed to use a Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) to map 70% of the Venusian surface down to a resolution of 390 to 985 feet (120 to 300 meters).

chapters.caption: Magellan — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Magellan get to Venus?
paragraphs: The Challenger disaster in January 1986 profoundly impacted the shuttle launch manifest into the 1990s, which included a number of planetary missions.
After three en route trajectory corrections (May 21, 1989, March 13, 1990, and July 25, 1990), Magellan arrived in Venus orbit on Aug. 10, 1990.

chapters.caption: Venus - Comparison of Venera and Magellan Resolutions

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Magellan taught us?
paragraphs: Beginning Sept. 15, 1990, the spacecraft began returning high-quality radar images of the Venusian terrain that showed evidence of volcanism, tectonic movement, turbulent surface winds, miles (kilometers) of lava channels, and pancake-shaped domes.

Magellan completed its first 243-day cycle (i.e., the time it took for Venus to rotate once under Magellan’s orbit) of radar mapping on May 15, 1991, providing the first clear views of 83.7% of the surface.

chapters.caption: Venus - Magellan and Arecibo Comparison

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Magellan now?
paragraphs: The spacecraft’s second mapping cycle, already beyond the original goals of the mission, ended on Jan. 15, 1992, raising coverage to 96%.
Magellan finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

paragraphs: Akatsuki is studying the atmosphere of Venus from orbit. Recovering from missed orbit insertion in 2010 and entering Venus orbit in 2015, Akatsuki is Japan’s first successful mission to explore another planet.
Akatsuki launched in 2010 (May 20, 2010), bound for Venus.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Akatsuki?
paragraphs: Meteorological information is obtained by globally mapping clouds and minor constituents successively with four cameras at ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths, detecting lightning with a high-speed imager, and observing the vertical structure of the atmosphere with radio science techniques.
The spacecraft was originally designated Planet-C, and is also known at t he Venus Climate Orbiter.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Akatsuki get to Venus?
paragraphs: Recovered from missed orbit insertion in 2010 and entered Venus orbit in 2015.
The equatorial elongated orbit with westward revolution matches the Venusian atmosphere, which rotates westward.

chapters.question: What has Akatsuki taught us?
paragraphs: Study weather patterns on Venus, confirm the presence of lightning in thick clouds and search for signs of active volcanism.
The systematic, continuous imaging observations will provide us with an unprecedented large dataset of the Venusian atmospheric dynamics.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Surveyor 3 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Surveyor 3 was the second in the Surveyor series to make a soft landing on the Moon. Based on the spacecraft’s surface sampling tests, scientists concluded the lunar surface was solid enough to hold the weight of an Apollo lunar module.
Surveyor 3 launched in 1967 (April 17, 1967), bound for the Moon.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Surveyor 3?
paragraphs: Surveyor 3 was the third engineering flight of the series, but for the first time carried a surface-sampling instrument that could reach up to 5 feet (1.5 meters) from the lander and could dig up to 7 inches (18 centimeters) deep.

The third time, the lander settled down to a soft-landing at 00:04:17 UT April 20, 1967, in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum at 3 degrees south latitude and 23.41 degrees west longitude.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Surveyor 3 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: Unlike the previous Surveyors, Surveyor 3 began its mission from parking orbit around Earth with a burn from the Centaur upper stage, now capable of multiple firings.
Bean landed the Intrepid Lunar Module approximately 197 yards (180 meters) from the inactive Surveyor 3 lander.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Surveyor 3 taught us?
paragraphs: Based on these experiments, scientists concluded that lunar soil had a consistency similar to wet sand, with a bearing strength of about 10 pounds per square inch (0.7 kilograms per square centimeter, or 98 kilopascals)— in other words, solid enough to support an Apollo Lunar Module.

During their second extra-vehicular activity (EVA) on Nov. 19, 1969, the astronauts walked over to Surveyor 3 and recovered parts, including the soil scoop and camera system, to allow scientists to evaluate the effects of nearly two-and-a-half years of exposure on the Moon’s surface.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Surveyor 1 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Surveyor 1 completed the first true soft-landing on the Moon. The mission was considered a complete success and demonstrated the technology necessary to achieve landing and operations on the lunar surface.
Surveyor 1 launched in 1966 (May 30, 1966), bound for the Moon.

chapters.question: What is Surveyor 1?
paragraphs: In January 1961, NASA selected Hughes Aircraft Company to build a series of seven soft-landing vehicles, each weighing about 750 pounds (340 kilograms), to “land gently on the Moon, perform chemical analyses of the lunar surface and subsurface and relay back to Earth television pictures of lunar features.”
These vehicles were to be designed and built under the technical direction of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and launched in the period of 1963-1966.

Touchdown coordinates were announced as 2.46 degrees south latitude and 43.32 degrees west longitude, just 9 miles (14 kilometers) from the planned target.

chapters.question: How did Lunar Orbiter 4 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: The imaging mission ended on the orbiter’s 34th orbit due to worsening readout difficulties.
In early June, controllers lowered the spacecraft’s orbit to match that of Lunar Orbiter 5 so that scientists could collect gravitational data in support of the latter mission.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Lunar Orbiter 4 taught us?
paragraphs: A potentially serious problem threatened the mission on May 13, 1967, when controllers found a problem with a camera thermal door that failed to close, leaking light onto exposed images.
Before losing contact on July 17, 1967, Lunar Orbiter 4 took the first photos of the lunar south pole and discovered a 149-mile (240-kilometer) long crustal fault on the far side.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Lunar Orbiter 4 now?
paragraphs: Since contact was lost before the controlled impact, the spacecraft naturally crashed onto the Moon on Oct. 6, 1967, due to gravitational anomalies.
Lunar Orbiter 4 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Topography of Earth's moon (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Lunar Orbiter 3 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Lunar Orbiter 3 was the final mission to photograph potential Apollo landing sites. A glitch prevented the spacecraft from relaying back all of its images, but it did meet all mission objectives. One of the images showed the Surveyor 2 lander on the lunar surface.
Lunar Orbiter 3 launched in 1967 (Feb. 5, 1967), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Lunar Orbiter 3?
paragraphs: Lunar Orbiter 3 was NASA’s final Lunar Orbiter mission to study potential Apollo landing sites, although its mission focused on site confirmation rather than site search.
For the mission, the spacecraft’s orbital inclination was increased to 21 degrees to ensure photography both north and south of the lunar equator.
chapters.imageAlt: Lunar Orbiter 3 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Lunar Orbiter 3 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Lunar Orbiter 3 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: The spacecraft arrived in lunar orbit after a 9-minute 2.5-second engine burn on Feb. 8, 1967, after a course correction.
About four days later, the spacecraft entered its operational 34 × 1,148-mile (55 × 1,847-kilometer) orbit at a 20.9-degree inclination.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Lunar Orbiter 3 taught us?
paragraphs: Lunar Orbiter 3 was also designed to obtain precision trajectory information for defining the lunar gravitational field, to measure micrometeoroid flux, and to measure radiation dosage levels around the Moon.

The photographs from the first three Lunar Orbiters allowed NASA scientists to pick eight preliminary landing sites for Apollo by early April 1967—including site 2 in the Sea of Tranquility where Apollo 11 would land and site 5 in the Ocean of Storms where Apollo 12 (and also Surveyor 3) would disembark.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Lunar Orbiter 3 now?
paragraphs: The spacecraft exposed 211 (out of a possible 212) frames of pictures by the time that imaging concluded Feb. 23.
Lunar Orbiter 3 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Topography of Earth's moon (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Lunar Orbiter 2 launched?
paragraphs: Like its predecessor, Lunar Orbiter 2 was designed primarily to collect images of the lunar surface, for safe landing sites for the Surveyor and Apollo missions. These included a spectacular oblique picture of Copernicus crater which was dubbed by the news media as one of the great pictures of the century.
Lunar Orbiter 2 launched in 1966 (Nov. 6, 1966), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Lunar Orbiter 2?
paragraphs: Lunar Orbiter 2’s mission was to photograph 13 primary and 17 secondary landings sites for the Apollo program in the northern region of the Moon’s near side equatorial area.
After a course correction on the way to the Moon, on Nov. 10, 1966, the spacecraft entered a 122 × 1,150-mile (196 × 1,850-kilometer) orbit around the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Lunar Orbiter 2 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Lunar Orbiter 2 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Lunar Orbiter 2 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: After 33 orbits, Lunar Orbiter 2 was moved to its photographic orbit with a perilune (closest point to the surface) of about 31 miles (49.7 kilometers).
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Lunar Orbiter 2 taught us?
paragraphs: On Dec. 8, 1966, after the main photographic mission was over, Lunar Orbiter 2 fired its main engine to change its orbital plane in order to provide tracking data of the Moon’s gravitational field over a wider swath.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Lunar Orbiter 2 now?
paragraphs: On Nov. 18, 1966, Lunar Orbiter 2 began its photography mission, returning excellent quality medium and high-resolution photographs, including the impact point of Ranger 8.
Lunar Orbiter 2 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Topography of Earth's moon (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Lunar Orbiter 1 launched?
paragraphs: The Lunar Orbiter 1 spacecraft was designed primarily to photograph smooth areas of the lunar surface for selection and verification of safe landing sites for the Surveyor and Apollo missions.
Lunar Orbiter 1 launched in 1966 (Aug. 10, 1966), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Lunar Orbiter 1?
paragraphs: The Lunar Orbiter program originated in response to the need to obtain detailed photographs of potential Apollo landing sites.
NASA planned to launch a series of three-axis stabilized spacecraft, each with four solar panels and a main engine (derived from an Apollo attitude control thruster) for lunar orbit insertion.
chapters.imageAlt: Lunar Orbiter 1 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Lunar Orbiter 1 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Lunar Orbiter 1 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: Lunar Orbiter 1 was launched into a parking orbit around Earth before its Agena upper stage fired at 20:04 UT to insert it on a translunar trajectory.

The vehicle also displayed higher than expected temperatures but successfully entered a 1,160 × 118-mile (1,866.8 × 189.1-kilometer) orbit around the Moon on Aug. 14, 1966, thus becoming the first U.S. spacecraft to do so.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Lunar Orbiter 1 taught us?
paragraphs: The narrow-angle pictures taken by this system provided resolution of 200 to 260 feet (60 to 80 meters), while the wide-angle photos showed resolutions up to 0.3 miles (0.5 kilometers).
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Lunar Orbiter 1 now?
paragraphs: By Aug. 28, 1966, Lunar Orbiter 1 had completed its main photography mission, having exposed a total of 205 frames, of which 38 were taken in the initial orbit and 167 in lower orbits, covering an area of 2 million square miles (5.18 million square kilometers).
Lunar Orbiter 1 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Kaguya launched?
paragraphs: Kaguya, originally named SELENE (Selenological and Engineering Explorer) was Japan’s second mission to explore the Moon from orbit. Kaguya created the most detailed topographical model to date. The mission carried two small satellites: Okina and Ouna.
Kaguya launched in 2007 (Sept. 14, 2007), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Kaguya?
paragraphs: In addition to the main orbiter, Kaguya, the mission included two small spin-stabilized sub-satellites, each weighing about 117 pounds (53 kilograms).

Originally slated for launch in 2003 but delayed to 2007 due to problems with the H-II launch vehicle, the probe was launched into a highly elliptical parking orbit of about 175 x 144,800 miles (282 × 232,960 kilometers).
chapters.imageAlt: Kaguya from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Kaguya — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Kaguya get to the Moon?
paragraphs: SELENE was renamed Kaguya, or Moon Princess, after launch as a result of a public poll.

The mission’s goal was to orbit the Moon to collect data on the origins and geological evolution of Earth’s only natural satellite, to study the lunar surface environment, and to carry out radio science experiments.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Kaguya taught us?
paragraphs: Kaguya’s other achievements included detecting gravity anomalies on both the near and the far side of the Moon (based on Doppler data from both Kaguya and the Okina satellite) and the first optical observation of the permanently shadowed interior of the Shackleton Crater.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Kaguya now?
paragraphs: Kaguya completed its original planned mission by late October 2008, with hopes to continue to March 2009 followed by impact in August 2009.
Kaguya finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Topography of Earth's moon (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Hiten / Hagoromo launched?
paragraphs: Hiten was Japan’s Earth orbiting satellite designed primarily to test and verify technologies for future lunar and planetary missions. The spacecraft carried a small satellite named Hagoromo that was released in the vicinity of the Moon.
Hiten / Hagoromo launched in 1990 (Jan. 24, 1990), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Hiten / Hagoromo?
paragraphs: This two-module Japanese spacecraft was designed to fly past the Moon and release an orbiter.
It was the first Japanese lunar mission, and also the first robotic lunar probe since the flight of the Soviet Luna 24 in 1976.
chapters.imageAlt: Hiten / Hagoromo from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Hiten / Hagoromo — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Hiten / Hagoromo get to the Moon?
paragraphs: Muses-A (for Mu-launched Space Engineering Satellite) was launched into a highly elliptical Earth orbit that intersected the Moon’s orbit.
After launch, the spacecraft, which was renamed Hiten, returned technical data on trajectory and optical navigation from an onboard computer.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Hiten / Hagoromo taught us?
paragraphs: Hiten / Hagoromo was sent to test technologies for future missions.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Hiten / Hagoromo now?
paragraphs: Although the maneuver successfully demonstrated the use of the swingby technique to enter lunar orbit, communication with Hagoromo was lost shortly after release.
Hiten / Hagoromo finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Topography of Earth's moon (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was LCROSS launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite (LCROSS) was launched with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to determine if water-ice exists in a permanently shadowed crater at the Moon’s south pole. As planned, LCROSS and its Centaur stage impacted the Moon on Oct. 9, 2009.
LCROSS launched in 2009 (June 18, 2009), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Stennis engineer part of LCROSS moon mission (NASA)
chapters.caption: Stennis engineer part of LCROSS moon mission

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is LCROSS?
paragraphs: The mission of the Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite (LCROSS), like the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), was to confirm the presence of water ice in a permanently shadowed crater at the Moon’s south pole.

Both spacecraft were part of NASA’s now-canceled Lunar Precursor Robotic Program and both missions were originally funded as part of NASA’s human spaceflight Constellation program to return humans to the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: LCROSS from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: LCROSS — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did LCROSS get to the Moon?
paragraphs: LCROSS was launched with LRO and traveled to the Moon as a co-manifested payload aboard the launch vehicle.

The Centaur upper stage entered a 112 × 129-mile (180 × 208-kilometer) parking orbit before firing again at 22:15 UT June 18 to reach a 121 × 219,800-mile (194 × 353,700-kilometer) orbit at a 28.2-degree inclination.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has LCROSS taught us?
paragraphs: The mission included impacting the Centaur upper stage on the surface of the Moon and then flying LCROSS through the debris plume about four minutes later to collect data on the soil.

A serious problem was discovered earlier, on Aug. 22, when mission controllers found that a sensor problem had caused the spacecraft to burn through 309 pounds (140 kilograms) of propellant, more than half of the amount remaining at the time.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is LCROSS now?
paragraphs: LCROSS also would impact a little later.
LCROSS finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe launched?
paragraphs: India’s Chandrayaan-1 played a crucial role in the discovery of water molecules on the Moon.
Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe launched in 2008 (Oct. 22, 2008), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe is an orbiter, impact built by ISRO to study the Moon. Its goal: orbit, then impact Earth's Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe — NASA imagery.

chapters.question: How did Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe get to the Moon?
paragraphs: Reaching the Moon takes patience: Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe cruised through deep space for months or years before it could start working.

chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe taught us?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe was sent to orbit, then impact Earth's Moon.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe now?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-1 / Moon Impact Probe finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Chandrayaan-2 launched?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-2 launched in 2019 (July 22, 2019), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Chandrayaan-2?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-2 is an orbiter, lander, rover built by ISRO to study the Moon. Its goal: land a rover on the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Chandrayaan-2 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Chandrayaan-2 — NASA imagery.

chapters.question: How did Chandrayaan-2 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: Reaching the Moon takes patience: Chandrayaan-2 cruised through deep space for months or years before it could start working.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Chandrayaan-2 taught us?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-2 was sent to land a rover on the Moon.

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Chandrayaan-2 now?
paragraphs: Chandrayaan-2 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s GRAIL mission flew twin spacecraft—Ebb and Flow—in tandem around the Moon to map variations in the lunar gravitational field. The probes generated the highest resolution gravity map of any celestial body to date. At the end of the mission, the probes were purposely crashed on the Moon.
GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) launched in 2011 (Sept. 10, 2011), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is GRAIL (Ebb and Flow)?
paragraphs: Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) was a dual-spacecraft mission that involved placing two identical spacecraft in orbit around the Moon to use high-quality gravitational field mapping to determine its internal structure.

As the two spacecraft flew over areas of increasing gravity, the probes moved slightly toward and away from each other, while an instrument measured changes in their relative velocity, providing key information on the Moon’s gravitational field.
chapters.imageAlt: GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) get to the Moon?
paragraphs: The GRAIL spacecraft was a design evolution of the U.S. Air Force’s Experimental Satellite System-11 (XSS-11) launched in 2005.
GRAIL made use of a low-energy translunar cruise that involved passing near the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point and then heading for a rendezvous with the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) taught us?
paragraphs: The mission was the 11th in NASA’s Discovery Program.
The process used for GRAIL was very similar to the one used by NASA’s Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE), which mapped variations in Earth’s gravity field from 2002 to 2017.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) now?
paragraphs: A second science phase, as part of the extended mission, was initiated Aug. 8, 2012.
GRAIL (Ebb and Flow) finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Explorer 49 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Explorer 49 was the final U.S. mission to the Moon for 21 years. The mission was successful and Explorer 49 studied low-frequency radio emissions from our solar system and beyond.
Explorer 49 launched in 1973 (June 10, 1973), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Explorer 49?
paragraphs: The spacecraft, part of a duo of Radio Astronomy Explorer (RAE) missions (the other being Explorer 48), was designed to conduct comprehensive studies of low-frequency radio emissions from the Sun, the Moon, the planets, and other galactic and extragalactic sources, while in a circular orbit around the Moon.

On June 18, 1973, the spacecraft jettisoned its main engine and, using its velocity control propulsion system, circularized its orbit to about 661 × 654 miles (1,063 × 1,052 kilometers) at a 38.7-degree inclination.
chapters.imageAlt: Explorer 49 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Explorer 49 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Explorer 49 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: After launch at 1 4:13:00 UT June 10, 1973, on a direct ascent trajectory to the Moon and a June 11 course correction, Explorer 49 fired its insertion motor on 07:21 UT June 15 to enter orbit around the Moon.
The spacecraft was the largest human-made object to orbit the Moon to date — with its deployed antennas measuring about 1,500 feet (457.2 meters or nearly half a kilometer!) tip-to-tip.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Explorer 49 taught us?
paragraphs: Explorer 49 was sent to study low-frequency radio emissions.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Explorer 49 now?
paragraphs: Explorer 49 was the final U.S. mission to the Moon for 21 years until NASA’s Clementine mission in 1994.
Explorer 49 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Explorer 35 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Explorer 35 studied the Moon from orbit for six years and discovered that the Moon has no magnetosphere, that solar wind particles impact directly onto the surface, and that the Moon creates a “cavity” in the solar wind stream. The satellite later impacted the lunar surface.
Explorer 35 launched in 1967 (July 19, 1967), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Explorer 35?
paragraphs: The spacecraft left Earth on a direct ascent trajectory and entered lunar orbit on July 21, 1967, after a 23-second burn.
The main engine separated 2 hours later, the spacecraft having entered an initial elliptical orbit of 497 × 4,780 miles (800 × 7,692 kilometers) at 147 degree inclination.
chapters.imageAlt: Explorer 35 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Explorer 35 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Explorer 35 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: The spacecraft, similar to Explorer 33, which had failed to achieve lunar orbit, found that the Moon has no magnetosphere, that solar wind particles impact directly onto the surface, and that the Moon creates a “cavity” in the solar wind stream.
Explorer 35 was launched by the 50th Thor Delta booster, of which only three had failed to date, giving it a 94% success rating.
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Explorer 35 taught us?
paragraphs: Explorer 35 was sent to orbit and study Earth's Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Gravity at the Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Explorer 35 now?
paragraphs: The lunar satellite later impacted on the surface, although the precise location remains unknown.
Explorer 35 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.
chapters.imageAlt: Topography of Earth's moon (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Explorer 33 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Explorer 33 was supposed to be the first U.S. spacecraft to orbit the Moon but the second stage accelerated too rapidly. Mission planners adopted an alternate mission and put the spacecraft into a highly elliptical Earth orbit that allowed it to come within about 22,000 miles (35,000 kilometers) of the Moon.
Explorer 33 launched in 1966 (July 1, 1966), bound for the Moon.
chapters.imageAlt: Moon North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Moon North Pole

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Explorer 33?
paragraphs: Instead, mission planners adopted an alternate mission that required the probe’s Thiokol TE-M-458 retro-rocket to fire about 6.5 hours after launch.
Under the new plan, the spacecraft was put into a highly elliptical Earth orbit of 279,000 × 19,000 miles (449,174 × 30,550 kilometers) at a 28.9-degree inclination.
chapters.imageAlt: Explorer 33 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Explorer 33 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Explorer 33 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: In this orbit, Explorer 33 was high enough to be perturbed by the Moon’s gravitation.

In its new orbit, Explorer 33 approached the Moon on its very first orbit to a distance of 22,000 miles (35,000 kilometers) with subsequent close approaches in Sept., Nov., and Dec. 1966 varying from 25,000 to 37,000 miles (40,000 to 60,000 kilometers).
chapters.imageAlt: The Moon's North Pole (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: The Moon's North Pole

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Explorer 33 taught us?
paragraphs: During this time, the probe returned key data on Earth’s magnetic tail, the interplanetary magnetic field, and radiation.
The mission was declared a success by Jan. 1, 1967, and the spacecraft continued to return useful data until Sept. 15, 1971.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Gravity at the Moon North Pole

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Explorer 33 now?
paragraphs: Explorer 33 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Topography of Earth's moon

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Clementine launched?
paragraphs: Clementine was the first U.S. spacecraft launched to the Moon in over 20 years. It was designed to test spacecraft components during extended exposure to space and to study the Moon and an asteroid. The mission succeeded in its lunar objectives, but a malfunction forced the asteroid flyby to be canceled.
Clementine launched in 1994 (Jan. 25, 1994), bound for the Moon.

chapters.caption: Farside View of Earth Moon as Seen by the Clementine Spacecraft

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Clementine?
paragraphs: Clementine was the first U.S. spacecraft launched to the Moon in over 20 years—since Explorer 49 in June 1973.

The spacecraft, also known as the Deep Space Program Science Experiment (DSPSE), was designed and built to demonstrate a set of lightweight technologies such as small-imaging sensors and lightweight gallium arsenide solar panels for future low-cost missions flown by the Department of Defense.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Clementine get to the Moon?
paragraphs: After launch, the spacecraft remained in a temporary parking orbit until Feb. 3, 1994, at which time a solid-propellant rocket ignited to send the vehicle to the Moon.

After two Earth flybys, Feb. 5 and Feb. 15, Clementine successfully entered an elliptical polar orbit (about 270 × 1,830 miles or 430 × 2,950 kilometers) around the Moon on Feb. 19, 1994, with a period of five days.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Clementine taught us?
paragraphs: In the process, it provided scientists with their first look at the total lunar landscape including polar regions.
On Dec. 3, 1996, the Department of Defense announced that Clementine data indicated that there was ice in the bottom of a permanently shadowed crater at the lunar South Pole.

chapters.caption: Clementine Images of Earth and Moon

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Clementine now?
paragraphs: The mission was terminated Aug. 8, 1994, when falling power supply levels no longer allowed clear telemetry exchange.
Clementine finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter launched in 2009 (June 18, 2009), bound for the Moon.

paragraphs: Ranger 2 was NASA’s second spacecraft launched to enter a highly elliptical Earth orbit that would take it into beyond the Moon to test new technologies and conduct experiments. paragraphs: Intended to be a lunar orbiter probe, its objectives were to place a highly instrumented probe in lunar orbit, to investigate the environment between the Earth and Moon, and to develop technology for controlling and maneuvering spacecraft from Earth.
Able 4B (Pioneer P-3) launched in 1959 (Nov. 26, 1959), bound for the Moon.

paragraphs: Two of the spacecraft had originally been slated for Venus orbit in June 1959, but mission planners redirected the missions after the success of the Soviet Automatic Interplanetary Station (Luna 3) mission.

All the scientific experiments and internal instrumentation were powered by nickel-cadmium batteries charged from 1,100 solar cells on four paddles, which made the vehicle resemble the recently-launched Explorer 6.

chapters.question: Why was Pioneer 4 launched?
paragraphs: Pioneer 4 was launched by the U.S. to photograph the Moon during a close flyby. It didn’t achieve that goal but it did become the first American spacecraft to escape Earth’s gravity and the nation’s first probe to enter heliocentric orbit.
Pioneer 4 launched in 1959 (Mar. 3, 1959), bound for the Moon.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Pioneer 4?
paragraphs: This was the last of five American lunar probes launched as part of a series during the International Geophysical Year, although the year officially ended a few months prior.
Although it did not achieve its primary objective to photograph the Moon during a close flyby, Pioneer 4 became the first U.S. spacecraft to reach Earth escape velocity.

chapters.question: How did Pioneer 4 get to the Moon?
paragraphs: A mechanism was on board to slow the spin-stabilized vehicle from its initial spin of 480 rpm down to 11 rpm about 11 hours after launch.

chapters.question: What has Pioneer 4 taught us?

Scientists received excellent data from the spacecraft that suggested the intensity of the upper belt of the Van Allen Belts had changed since Pioneer 3 (probably attributable to a recent solar flare) and that there might be a third belt at a higher altitude.

paragraphs: Pioneer 3 was the first of two U.S. Army launches to the Moon. The spacecraft failed to fly by the Moon and go into a heliocentric orbit as planned, but it did return valuable data about the Van Allen radiation belts that encircle Earth.

Two special 0.21-ounce (6-gram) weights were to be spun out on 5 foot (1.5-meter) wires to reduce spin to 6 rpm once the mission was underway.

paragraphs: NASA’s Mariner 8 (also called Mariner-H and Mariner-71H) was the first in a pair of American spacecraft intended to explore the physical and dynamic characteristics of Mars from Martian orbit.

The overall goals for the spacecraft were to search for an environment that could support life; to collect data on the origins and evolution of Mars; to gather information on planetary physics, geology, planetology, and cosmology; and to provide data that could aid future spacecraft such as the Viking landers.

paragraphs: Near its discarded heat shield, Opportunity discovered an unusual basketball-sized rock in January 2005 (named the “Heat Shield Rock”) that turned out to be an iron-nickel meteorite.

paragraphs: A Japanese (JAXA) mission to travel to Mars and survey the Red Planet’s two moons, Phobos and Deimos. The spacecraft will explore both moons and collect a sample of Phobos and bring it to Earth.
MMX launched in 2026 (Oct. 20, 2026), bound for Mars.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is MMX?
paragraphs: NASA’s Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma Ray and Neutrons (MEGANE) instrument will play a major role in the MMX mission, which aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons, Phobos and Deimos, and deliver a sample from Phobos to Earth.
MMX is an orbiter, sample return built by JAXA to study Mars. Its goal: clarify the origin of the two Martian moons and the evolution process of Mars, Phobos and Deimos.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has MMX taught us?
paragraphs: Scientists suspect the asteroid-sized bodies either are remnants of an ancient collision between Mars and a large impactor or are themselves asteroids captured by Mars’ gravity.

By measuring the energies of neutrons and gamma rays emitted from the surface of Phobos, MEGANE will let MMX “see” the elemental composition of the moon’s surface and help peg the likely origin of the moon.

paragraphs: India’s Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM)—or Mangalyaan (Hindi for “Mars Craft”)—was the country’s first mission to the Red Planet. The mission goal was to test key technologies for interplanetary exploration and to use its five science instruments to study the Martian surface and atmosphere from orbit.
Mars Orbiter Mission launched in 2013 (Nov. 5, 2013), bound for Mars.

Mars Express launched in 2003 (June 2, 2003), bound for Mars.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Galileo launched?
paragraphs: Galileo changed the way we look at our solar system. When the spacecraft plunged into Jupiter's crushing atmosphere on Sept. 21, 2003, it was being deliberately destroyed to protect one of its own discoveries—a possible ocean beneath the icy crust of the moon Europa.
Galileo launched in 1989 (Oct. 18, 1989), bound for Jupiter.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Juno launched?
paragraphs: Since it arrived at Jupiter in 2016, NASA’s Juno spacecraft has been probing beneath the dense, forbidding clouds encircling the giant planet — the first orbiter to peer so closely. It’s looking to answer questions about the origin and evolution of Jupiter, our solar system, and giant planets across the cosmos.
Juno launched in 2011 (Aug. 5, 2011), bound for Jupiter.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Juno?
paragraphs: The spacecraft found previously unseen networks of vast storms swirling around Jupiter’s poles, active volcanoes and lakes of lava on the tempestuous moon, Io, and answers to a decades-old question about winds on Jupiter extending hundreds of miles toward the planet’s interior.
Juno is an orbiter built by NASA to study Jupiter. Its goal: explore the Jovian system.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Juno get to Jupiter?
paragraphs: After enduring a five-year, 1.7 billion-mile journey from Earth, and evading showers of the most punishing radiation outside the Sun, Juno has provided breathtaking images and breakthrough discoveries from Jupiter and its moons.
From its very first orbit, stretching across 53 days from Jupiter’s cloud tops to the frontiers of its magnetic field, Juno has upended our views of the gas giant and its surroundings.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Pioneer 11 launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Pioneer 11, a sister spacecraft to Pioneer 10, was the first spacecraft to study Saturn up close.
Pioneer 11 launched in 1973 (April 6, 1973), bound for Jupiter.
chapters.imageAlt: Pioneer 11 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Pioneer 11 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Pioneer 11?
paragraphs: Pioneer 11, the sister spacecraft to Pioneer 10, was the first human-made object to fly past Saturn and also returned the first pictures of the polar regions of Jupiter.

After boost by the TE-M-364-4 engine, the spacecraft sped away from Earth at a velocity of about 32,000 miles per hour (51,800 kilometers per hour), thus equaling the speed of its predecessor, Pioneer 10.
chapters.imageAlt: Pioneer 11 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Pioneer 11 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Pioneer 11 get to Jupiter?
paragraphs: During the outbound journey, there were a number of malfunctions on the spacecraft—including the momentary failure of one of the RTG booms to deploy, a problem with an attitude control thruster, and the partial failure of the asteroidal dust detector—but none of these jeopardized the mission.
Soon, on April 26, 1974, it performed a midcourse correction (after an earlier one on April 11, 1973) to guide it much closer to Jupiter than Pioneer 10 and to ensure a polar flyby.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Crescent Jupiter with the Great Red Spot

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Pioneer 11 taught us?
paragraphs: Pioneer 11 detected Saturn’s bow shock on Aug. 31, 1979, about 932,000 miles (1.5 million kilometers) out from the planet, thus providing the first conclusive evidence of the existence of Saturn’s magnetic field.
The images of Saturn’s moon Titan (at a resolution of 112 miles or 180 kilometers) showed a featureless orange fuzzy satellite.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Jupiter's Great Red Spot, Spotted

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Pioneer 11 now?
paragraphs: The mission ended in 1995 and Pioneer 11 is on a trajectory to take it out of the solar system.
Pioneer 11 finished its mission. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.title: The Beginning
chapters.question: Why was Pioneer 10 launched?
paragraphs: Pioneer 10 was NASA’s first mission to the outer planets. The mission was a spectacular success and the spacecraft notched a series of firsts unmatched by any other robotic spacecraft to date.
Pioneer 10 launched in 1972 (March 2, 1972), bound for Jupiter.
chapters.imageAlt: Pioneer 10 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Pioneer 10 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Pioneer 10?
paragraphs: After launch by a three-stage version of the Atlas Centaur (with a TE-M-364-4 solid propellant engine modified from the Surveyor lander), Pioneer 10 reached a maximum escape velocity of 32,110 miles per hour (51,682 kilometers per hour), faster than any previous human-made object at that point in time.
On July 15, 1972, the spacecraft entered the asteroid belt, emerging in February 1973 after a voyage of about 271 million miles (435 million kilometers).
chapters.imageAlt: Pioneer 10 from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Pioneer 10 — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Pioneer 10 get to Jupiter?
paragraphs: Controllers carried out two course corrections, on March 7 and March 26, the latter to ensure an occultation experiment with Jupiter’s moon Io.
In conjunction with Pioneer 9 (in solar orbit), on Aug. 7, Pioneer 10 recorded details of one of the most violent solar storms in recent record.
chapters.imageAlt: An artist's concept of the Pioneer 10 spacecraft. (NASA)
chapters.caption: An artist's concept of the Pioneer 10 spacecraft.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Pioneer 10 taught us?
paragraphs: During this period, the spacecraft encountered some asteroid hits, although fewer than expected, and also measured the intensity of Zodiacal light in interplanetary space.
Based on the data, scientists identified plasma in Jupiter’s magnetic field.

chapters.caption: Pioneer 10 Ganymede

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Pioneer 10 now?
paragraphs: A final attempt to contact Pioneer 10 on March 4, 2006, failed.
Pioneer 10 finished its mission in 1997. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.question: Why was Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe launched?
paragraphs: NASA’s Galileo spacecraft carried an atmospheric entry probe that was released July 13, 1995, when the main spacecraft was still about 50 million miles (80 million kilometers) from Jupiter. The probe hit the atmosphere Dec. 7, 1995, and returned valuable data for 58 minutes.
Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe launched in 1989 (Oct. 18, 1989), bound for Jupiter.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe?
paragraphs: NASA’s Galileo mission to Jupiter – one of the agency’s most ambitious deep space missions –carried a 743-pound (337-kilogram) probe designed to return data as it entered the Jovian atmosphere by parachute.
The Galileo atmospheric entry probe was based on the design of the large probe of the Pioneer Venus multi-probe.
chapters.imageAlt: Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe from the NASA archive
chapters.caption: Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe get to Jupiter?
paragraphs: Having completed its 35th orbit around Jupiter and after accompanying the planet for three-quarters of a circuit around the Sun, Galileo flew into the atmosphere at a velocity of 30 miles per second (48.2 kilometers per second), just south of the equator, on Sept. 21, 2003, at 18:57 UT.
chapters.imageAlt: Jupiter's Great Red Spot, Spotted (NASA archive view)
chapters.caption: Archive view: Jupiter's Great Red Spot, Spotted

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe taught us?
paragraphs: The probe returned valuable data for 58 minutes as it plunged into the Jovian cauldron.

Data, originally transmitted to the main spacecraft and later transmitted back to Earth, indicated an intense radiation belt about 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) above Jupiter’s clouds, few organic compounds, and winds as high as about half a mile per second (640 meters per second).

chapters.title: Mission Today
chapters.question: Where is Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe now?
paragraphs: Because Galileo had not been sterilized, to prevent contamination, it was decided to have the vehicle burn up in the Jovian atmosphere after its mission ended instead of risking impact on one of Jupiter’s moons such as Europa.
Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe finished its mission in 1995. The spacecraft is quiet, but its pictures and measurements are still used by scientists today.

chapters.question: Why was Cassini-Huygens launched?
paragraphs: Cassini was a sophisticated robotic spacecraft sent to study Saturn and its complex system of rings and moons in unprecedented detail. It was one of the most ambitious efforts ever mounted in planetary exploration.
Cassini-Huygens launched in 1997 (Oct. 15, 1997), bound for Saturn.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft
chapters.question: What is Cassini-Huygens?
paragraphs: It became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, beginning a mission that yielded troves of new insights over more than a decade.
Cassini-Huygens is an orbiter, probe built by NASA to study Saturn.

chapters.caption: Cassini-Huygens — NASA imagery.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.question: How did Cassini-Huygens get to Saturn?
paragraphs: Reaching Saturn takes patience: Cassini-Huygens cruised through deep space for months or years before it could start working.

chapters.caption: Archive view: Saturn Rings

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.question: What has Cassini-Huygens taught us?
paragraphs: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute Science at Saturn Before Cassini, we had only brief glimpses of the discoveries awaiting us at Saturn.
The Saturnian system proved to be rich ground for exploration and discoveries, and Cassini’s science findings changed the course of future planetary exploration.
